title: Karmic tail 9-12-3 in the destiny matrix: “the Lonely Woman”, the unspoken request and a hostess at her own table

seo.title: Karmic Tail 9-12-3 “The Lonely Woman” in the Destiny Matrix
seo.description: 9-12-3 is the only tail with the Empress at the root and the Hanged Man in the middle. A ten-second date check, Martha and Mary, and eight practices.

short: Popular destiny matrix readings call the 9-12-3 tail “the Lonely Woman”, or less often “Female Loneliness”. Gender plays no part in the calculation: men and women get this tail equally. And the loneliness in it is usually not about an empty flat. It is loneliness among your own people: the person feeds everyone, makes everyone comfortable, waits and puts up with things, and stays silent about what they need themselves. The entry into the script is the Hermit (9): coping with everything important alone and without words. The mechanism is the Hanged Man (12): the unspoken request hangs in the air, and life is put on pause, waiting for someone to guess. The root is the Empress (3): abundance, home, fertility, and the task of making sure that this abundance has room for the hostess too. 9-12-3 is the only one of the 26 tails where the Empress stands at the root and the Hanged Man works as the mechanism. It comes up for only one sum of the birth-date numbers — 30. And everyone who has it has the Lovers (6), the card of the couple, in the centre of the chart. So the main question of this tail is not “how do I stop being alone” but how to sit down at your own table: ask out loud, take your share and stop waiting for others to guess.

sections.h2: Do you have the 9-12-3 tail: a ten-second check
paragraphs: The tail depends entirely on one number — the sum of the first three arcana of the matrix. So you can find 9-12-3 without a calculator.

ol: **Day arcanum** — your day of birth. If it is greater than 22, add its digits: 25 → 7, 29 → 11, 30 → 3, 31 → 4.
**Year arcanum** — the sum of the digits of the year. If the result is greater than 22, add the digits again: 1977 → 24 → 6, 1985 → 23 → 5.

paragraphs: Add up the three numbers. If you get **exactly 30**, you have 9-12-3. Any other sum means a different tail: there is no other way to 9-12-3.

ul: 29.03.1987: 11 + 3 + 7 = 21 → not this one. That is 9-3-21: the same entry and the same centre, but the Empress stands in the middle, not at the root.
10.07.1984: 10 + 7 + 22 = 39 → not this one. That is 18-3-12: the same Empress and Hanged Man, only with their roles swapped.

paragraphs: If your chart is already calculated, it is even simpler. Look at the bottom corner — point D, the “karmic task”. If it holds 3, you have 9-12-3. No other tail has a 3 in the bottom corner.

Why this works. The sum 30 reduces into the bottom corner of the chart: 3 + 0 = 3, the Empress. The centre E is the same sum plus the corner: 30 + 3 = 33 → 3 + 3 = 6, the Lovers. After that there are no options left: the entry M = D + E = 3 + 6 = 9, the middle N = D + M = 3 + 9 = 12. This was checked by going through all 73,414 dates from 1900 to 2100.
Read the scheme from top to bottom, from the centre to the corner:
The sums whose digits finally add up to 3 — 12, 21, 30, 39 and 48 — all give the Lovers in the centre. But only one of them gives the 9-12-3 tail:
A common mistake when counting by hand is to reduce 21 or 39 to 3. Only sums greater than 22 are reduced, so 21 stays the twenty-first arcanum. And 39 gives 3 + 9 = 12.
The same arithmetic leads to facts you won’t find in popular readings:

ul: **This is more a tail of mothers and grandmothers than of children.** Since 1900, 9-12-3 has come up on 4.3% of dates — roughly one in twenty-three. That is 9th place out of 26. But the later the year of birth, the rarer it gets:

paragraphs: Among people born from 2000 to 2025, 9-12-3 drops to 16th place out of 26. The reason is arithmetic. To reach 30, the day and the month have to make up “30 minus the year arcanum”. Years of the 20th century usually have a medium or large arcanum, so there is not much to make up. In 1951 and 1960 (arcanum 16) you need 14, and that works for 21 dates a year, the maximum. Years of the 2000s have a small arcanum, so there is a lot to make up. In 2000 (arcanum 2) you need 28, and only seven dates manage it, one a month from June to December: 22 June, 21 July, 20 August, 19 September, 18 October, 17 November and 16 December.

ul: **There has never been a year without this tail.** Since 1900, every year has had at least seven dates with 9-12-3.

**It is unique on two counts at once.** Of the 26 tails, only this one has the Empress at the root. In the others she is the entry (3-7-22, 3-22-19, 3-13-10) or the mechanism (9-3-21, 18-3-12). And only here does the Hanged Man work as the mechanism. In other tails he is the entry (12-16-4, 12-19-7) or the root (18-3-12).

**3-12-9 is the same tail.** Some sites write this tail as 3-12-9 and call it “Female Loneliness”. These are the same three points, read from the outer corner towards the centre. There is no separate 3-12-9 tail: a 9 in the bottom corner gives only 9-18-9 and 18-9-9.

sections.h2: Why “the Lonely Woman”: the name, the legends and what they have in common
paragraphs: In the most widespread list of karmic tail names, 9-12-3 is called “the Lonely Woman”. You can read this name straight from the cards. “Lonely” is the Hermit at the entry, a figure who stands alone. “Woman” is the Empress at the root. In Waite she is “the fruitful mother of thousands”, “the Earthly Paradise” and “all that is symbolized by the visible house of man”. And between them stands the Hanged Man — what keeps them apart. The tail tells how home, care and love end up cut off from the one who creates them.
The tail has several past-life legends, and all of them are about love that had nowhere to go.

ul: **Waiting without news.** The most detailed version: a woman loved, but her beloved vanished. He went off to war, on a trading voyage, or simply disappeared. No news came. She never found out whether he had died or left her, and she turned others away, because a new love felt like a betrayal to her. In some retellings she remained childless or could not love her own children.
**A nun or recluse** who gave up worldly joys.
**A woman who sacrificed everything for a man** and was left alone.
**A domineering woman** who suppressed her tenderness and used people for her own ends.
**A closed person** who considered their knowledge exceptional and could not reach agreement with others.

paragraphs: The legends cannot be checked: neither numbers nor cards say anything about past lives. But all the legends share a common denominator, and it matches the cards exactly. Love and care (the Empress) have frozen (the Hanged Man) in solitude (the Hermit). Waiting for someone who will not return. Giving everything to someone who left. Locking tenderness away in a cell or hiding it under domineering. Keeping knowledge to yourself.

The most detailed legend, about waiting without news, has a precise name in psychology. In the 1970s the American family therapist Pauline Boss talked with the wives of pilots missing in action in Vietnam. She called their state **ambiguous loss**. It is a loss without certainty: the person is gone, but you cannot call them dead. You cannot grieve — what if they are alive? You cannot move on either — what if they come back? Boss showed that such a loss freezes grief: a person gets stuck and can move neither backwards nor forwards. The Hanged Man, “life in suspension”, captures this in a single image.

Even more important is the second kind of ambiguous loss that Boss described. The person is physically present but psychologically absent. A husband who is at home every evening but not with you. Someone close who has lived for years in their work, a bottle or their phone. Popular readings of 9-12-3 describe exactly this: in a couple, the person feels unloved and unneeded, and the partners they choose seem to be forever absent. Our reading: the legend of the vanished beloved is not so much about a past life as about a recognisable loneliness in this one. Waiting for someone who is both there and not there.

This legend has an unexpected conversation partner — the root card itself. Benebell Wen mentions the speculation that the Empress may have been inspired by Saint Adelaide, a 10th-century empress, and lists whom she is considered the patron saint of: empresses, princesses, brides, parenthood, widows, second marriages, women in large families, and also abuse victims, prisoners and exiles. Behind this list stands a life story. At 19 Adelaide was widowed: her husband, King Lothair of Italy, was poisoned, according to the widespread version. She refused to marry the son of his successor, spent four months imprisoned in a castle on Lake Garda, escaped, hid in the marshes and in 951 married a second time — Otto I. Eleven years later she became empress. And at the end of her life she withdrew to the convent she had founded at Selz.

Wen only speaks of speculation, and we do not claim that the card was drawn from Adelaide. But the coincidence is worth noticing. At the root of a tail whose legend is widowhood without news and the refusal of a new love stands a card linked to the patron saint of widows and second marriages. Our reading: the Empress does not cancel either faithfulness or grief. She is about life bearing fruit again after a loss, and even after imprisonment. And there is solitude in her story too, but it comes at the end of a full life, not instead of it.

sections.h2: Doubly careful: what links the Hermit and the Hanged Man
paragraphs: If you put Waite’s descriptions of the tail’s three cards side by side, you see a detail that is easy to miss. In his divinatory list the Hermit has “prudence, circumspection”, and the Hanged Man has “wisdom, circumspection, discernment”. The word circumspection is shared by the two cards. And this is no accident of translation. In the history of the Tarot both cards were credited with the same virtue — prudence. Éliphas Lévi gave it to the Hermit. The Hanged Man, as Waite writes, was also supposed to represent prudence. Waite himself disputed both attributions, but the shared word remained in his list.
The Empress, in the same list, opens with “fruitfulness, action, initiative”. This is the opposite pole: not to look around, but to begin.

Our reading. The circumspection of people with 9-12-3 is real. They truly know how to foresee, to wait, to save their strength and not to rush after the first impulse. But in this tail it stands twice in a row, and it stands before the Empress, that is, before what calls for an impulse. Before giving birth to anything — a request, a wish, a celebration for themselves — the person checks twice. “What if they say no?” — that is the Hermit. “I’ll wait, maybe they’ll guess on their own” — that is the Hanged Man. While the checks go on, the moment passes. **The entry and mechanism of the tail are two kinds of caution in a row. The root is a card that is never cautious.**

There is a second hint too. Describing the Hermit, Waite rethinks the prudence that Lévi assigned to him. For Waite, prudence is “the economy which follows the line of least resistance”, “a doctrine of divine parsimony and conservation of energy, because of the stress, the terror and the manifest impertinences of this life”. Its axiom is Waste not, want not. In these lines it is easy to recognise the first reaction of 9-12-3. Don’t waste energy on a request that may not be heard. Follow the line of least resistance: “it’s easier to do it myself”. Shield yourself from the stress and impertinence of the world behind a closed door.

But Waite goes on. True prudence, he writes, is concerned with the one thing needful. In Russian these words are known in their Church Slavonic form, yedinoye na potrebu; English readers know them from the King James Bible: “one thing is needful”. They come from the Gospel story of Martha and Mary, and it is hard to find a parable that fits 9-12-3 better. We will come back to it below.

sections.h2: How the circle works: “I’ll do it myself” — “I’ll wait” — a feast without its hostess
paragraphs: Below is a scene, step by step. It is made up and does not describe everyone who has this tail.
In two days it is Mum’s milestone birthday, and there will be twelve guests. As always, Lena is doing the cooking.

**Entry — the Hermit: “I’ll do it myself.”** Her sister offered to bring the salads, her husband asked what to buy. “No need, I’ll do it myself, it’s quicker.” This is not pride but a habit that once proved itself: ask, and they’ll say no or do it wrong, and explaining takes longer than doing. This is where the tail begins. When something becomes personal — a need, tiredness, a wish, a grievance — the first move is always the same: take it inside and deal with it alone. In Waite’s divinatory list the Hermit has “prudence, circumspection”. And reversed, among other things, “concealment”, “fear” and “unreasoned caution”. Both can be recognised here.

**Mechanism — the Hanged Man: “I’ll wait until they notice.”** On the day of the party Lena doesn’t sit down. “In a minute, let me just bring out the main course”, “sit, sit, I’ll do it.” Someone says: “Oh, just sit down already!” — “In a minute.” She is waiting. Not for them to insist, but for them to see how much she has done and how tired she is, and to get up and go to the sink themselves. Her hands are like the hanged man’s on Waite’s card: tied behind her back. With hands like that you cannot take a plate for yourself and you cannot ask. Time stops for her: the party goes on in the living room, and she is in the kitchen. Inside, a tally is growing: “nobody offered”, “my sister didn’t even clear the plates”. The Hanged Man is the card of sacrifice; the word is in Waite’s divinatory list. But reversed, the same card has “selfishness”, and Wen cautions not to confuse martyrdom with selfishness. In this tail the sacrifice is silent but not free. It comes with a bill that nobody has seen.

**Root — the Empress: a feast without its hostess.** And the party is a success. Everyone is well fed, Mum is happy, the guests praise the pie. Here she is, the Empress: abundance, home, “fruitfulness, action, initiative”. This is the real gift of a person with 9-12-3: around them everything grows and blooms. But in the script the abundance goes to everyone except the hostess. Wen notes that the cushions the Empress sits on denote comfort. The Empress on the card is sitting down. The hostess of this tail is not.

**Repeat.** Late in the evening Lena washes the dishes alone. Her husband says: “Leave it, I’ll do it tomorrow.” — “All done.” That night she is silent, and the next morning she answers in monosyllables. “What’s wrong?” — “Nothing.” The bill has never been presented, so nobody can pay it. The tail draws its conclusion: asking is pointless, it’s easier to do it myself. By the next party the circle will start again from the Hermit. And with each turn the person gets better at needing nobody.

**In this tail, loneliness is made not of the absence of people but of unspoken requests.** The arithmetic of the tail says the same thing: the Hanged Man here is built from the Empress and the Hermit, 3 + 9 = 12. Our reading of this sum: care that is kept silent ends up hanging in the air.

The same pattern can be recognised in other settings too. An employee does the work of three and waits for years for her boss to offer a promotion himself. The mother of grown-up children waits for weeks for a call but doesn’t call herself: “I don’t want to impose.” A woman has been waiting for five years for a man to finally make up his mind. A man carries the whole family, silently waits for gratitude, and when none comes, retreats to the garage. Everywhere it is the same move: cope alone — wait to be noticed — give everything except yourself.

sections.h2: The Hostess, the Waiting One, the Recluse: one and the same tail
paragraphs: The legends of 9-12-3 sound as if they were about different women: a nun, a widow without news, a domineering mistress of the house, a victim. Life shows that these are modes of one script. In each, one of the three cards sounds louder than the others.

head: The Hostess
The Waiting One
The Recluse
Tail worked through
rows: warmth, reliability and a silent reproach
a person who is easy to take care of in return

paragraphs: **The Hostess** is the most recognisable form, and the Empress sounds loudest in it. The house runs, children and parents are fed, colleagues are covered, everyone has everything. Waite calls the Empress refugium peccatorum, “the refuge of sinners”, and “the fruitful mother of thousands”. The Hostess of this tail really does become a refuge for many, only she herself has no refuge. She is lonely not because there is nobody around, but because everybody is around — and nobody knows that she needs something too. Popular readings describe it like this: even in a couple the woman feels unneeded, and over time she starts playing the mother to her partner. There is nothing surprising here: someone who is cared for like a child behaves like a child.

**The Waiting One** is the form from the legend, and the Hanged Man sounds loudest in it. Life is on pause until some event. “When he leaves his wife.” “When the children grow up.” “When he finally understands.” “When I retire, I’ll live for myself.” The waiting can last for years and look like faithfulness or patience. Sometimes it really is faithfulness. But if time passes and the pause does not end, it is worth remembering what Waite insisted on. The hanged man’s tree is living, with leaves on it, and the whole figure means “life in suspension, but life and not death”.

Dickens described the extreme form of the Waiting One in “Great Expectations”. Miss Havisham was jilted on her wedding day, and she stopped all the clocks in the house at the minute the letter came — twenty minutes to nine. For decades she sits in her wedding dress, with only one shoe on, and in the next room the wedding cake stands on the table under cobwebs. She raises her adopted daughter to break men’s hearts: care becomes a weapon of revenge. This is the Hanged Man without what Waite insisted on: Havisham’s tree has withered. If your life has stopped clocks — a decision put off “until he…” — that is the first place to look.

**The Recluse** is the reversed form, and the Hermit sounds loudest in it. The person has gone unheard so many times that they stopped asking altogether. “I don’t need anyone”, “it’s calmer on my own”, “they’re all the same”. Popular readings attribute to this tail a distrust of people and an expectation of a catch, and one of the legends — a habit of shutting oneself off, considering one’s knowledge exceptional. Wen writes that there are two ways of interpreting the Hermit’s lantern: as light shone in the darkness for others — or as one’s own light, by which a person sees the world in their own way. The Recluse lives in the second. It looks like freedom from the script, but the script is the same. The request no longer hangs in the air only because it was cancelled in advance.

The forms take turns. Years as the Hostess end with the words “enough, now I’ll live for myself”, and the person turns into the Recluse. Then a new love appears, and the Recluse becomes the Waiting One. These are not three different people but one bottom ray of the chart in different years.

sections.h2: The hidden fourth card: everyone with 9-12-3 has the Lovers in the centre
paragraphs: “9-12-3 with 6 in the centre” is a common question, and the answer is simple: it can’t be any other way. The sum 30 always gives the centre 33 → 6. Everyone who has this tail has the Lovers in the centre of the matrix.

In the method, the centre is the comfort zone, the state a person returns to when nothing is demanded of them. And in the centre of the tail called “the Lonely Woman” stands the most coupled card in the deck. In Waite it is a man and a woman “unveiled before each other”, and “the card of human love”. Wen writes that the card represents partnership with one other person, and she puts the emphasis on choice. **The loneliness of 9-12-3 is not a character trait but a script.** The character shows in the centre: a person with this tail blossoms in closeness, in mutuality, where they have been chosen and where they have chosen for themselves. The script is what keeps them from stepping into that closeness.
And now the most curious part. The whole tail is built out of the Empress. The root D equals 3, and each next card comes from adding the Empress to the previous one:

ul: **The Lovers = the Empress + the Empress.** The centre equals 33, and 33 reduces to 3 + 3 = 6.
**The Hermit = the Empress + the Lovers** (3 + 6 = 9).
**The Hanged Man = the Empress + the Hermit** (3 + 9 = 12).
And one more formula, from the energy chart: **the Hanged Man = the Lovers + the Lovers** (6 + 6 = 12). Everyone who has this tail has Manipura equal to 6-6-12.

paragraphs: What follows is our reading, not a rule of the method. Two kinds of care that meet each other make love: the Lovers are when both take care. Care and love that find no answer lead inwards. People withdraw into the loneliness of this tail not from a lack of love but from a surplus of it that had nowhere to go. Care plus silence hangs in the air. And love that one person carries for two hangs in the air as well.

This arithmetic points to the way out more precisely than any advice. The centre of the tail is not “care more” but 3 + 3, care in both directions. **The 9-12-3 tail doesn’t need to learn to love. It needs to learn to take.**

sections.h2: Where else 9, 12 and 3 sound in your chart
paragraphs: The arithmetic of the tail places its cards in other spots of the matrix too. Here is what everyone with 9-12-3 has in common, without exception:

head: Where in the matrix
What everyone with 9-12-3 has
rows: 6-6-12 — The Lovers, The Lovers, The Hanged Man

paragraphs: An honest caveat. Svadhisthana’s Energy and the entry of the relationship line are the same point M as the entry of the tail. Muladhara’s Energy is the same point D as its root. The method reads these points in several places. That does not make them new coincidences, but it does show where else the tail sounds. Manipura 6-6-12 occurs in every tail with the Lovers in the centre, that is, also in 9-3-21 and 18-3-12.

**Manipura 6-6-12: a will that waits for the other one.** The row of status, will and money is made up of two cards of the couple and the Hanged Man. Our reading: decisions here are made with an eye on someone else — a partner, family, team. While the other person agrees, things move. When the other is silent or drags their feet, the decision hangs in the air, and the person lives for years in “let’s think about it some more” mode. The Lovers plus the Lovers give the Hanged Man: whoever decides for two and waits for the other’s consent is the one left hanging.

**Svadhisthana with the Hermit: joy in quiet.** For everyone with 9-12-3, the row of joy, children and creativity is fed by the Hermit. Joy more often comes to such people in solitude: in handicrafts, a garden, a book, a long walk, quiet work where nobody rushes them. This is a resource, not a flaw. There is just one risk: joy that is shared with no one, and creative work that sits in a drawer for years. The numbers say nothing about whether a person will have children. “Children” in the name of the row is a theme, not a forecast.

**Muladhara with the Empress: support in abundance.** For everyone, the row of body and support is fed by the Empress. Stability comes to these people from a full house, good food, a garden, warmth, things that bring joy. An important clarification: abundance becomes support when the hostess gets her share too. If everything goes to others, the support turns into a duty.

**The Hermit at the entry to love.** Point M, the entry of the tail, also opens the relationship line M–R1–R. So for everyone with 9-12-3, closeness begins with the Hermit: take a good look, wait, don’t show right away what you need yourself. For people born in 1905, 1914, 1923, 1932, 1941 and 1950, the relationship line repeats the tail entirely: 9-12-3. These are years with arcanum 15, and today such people are mostly found among grandmothers and grandfathers.

**A mirror for those born in March.** Everyone with 9-12-3 who was born in March has the talent line on the top ray equal to 3-12-9. These are the same cards in the same arrangement as on the bottom ray: the Empress at the outer corner, the Hanged Man in the middle, the Hermit next to the centre. For example, for the date 22.03.1985 the top and bottom rays of the chart are identical. This is not a second tail: the top ray is read as talent. Our reading: what works as a pause and silence in the tail becomes, in the talent line, a gift for carrying something to term — quietly and without haste — until it comes out into the world as fruit. For holders of the tail born in December the talent line is 12-3-18, the same Empress and Hanged Man, but with the Moon.
**Neighbours by centre: 9-3-21 and 18-3-12.** All three tails with the Lovers in the centre contain the Empress, and they are easy to confuse. What sets them apart is the role of care.

ul: In **9-3-21** (“the Overseer”) care is the mechanism. The person sees danger and covers it with care, and the care turns into supervision. The root is the World.
In **18-3-12** (“Physical Suffering”) care is the mechanism too: it is used to drown out fear for the body. The root is the Hanged Man.

In **9-12-3** care stands at the root, that is, it is a task, not a method. The Hanged Man here is not the root, as in 18-3-12, but the mechanism. The two tails hold the same cards with their roles swapped. In 18-3-12 you have to learn to accept the pause. In 9-12-3, to come out of it.

sections.h2: The parable: Martha, Mary and “the one thing needful”
paragraphs: The parallel below is ours, not part of the method’s tradition. But Waite himself gives the hint: his words about true prudence, which is concerned with “the one thing needful”, come from the Gospel of Luke. And the story they come from reads like a detailed map of the 9-12-3 tail.

Jesus and his disciples come to a village, and “a certain woman named Martha received him into her house”. Martha has a sister, Mary, “which also sat at Jesus’ feet, and heard his word”. “But Martha was cumbered about much serving” — and at last she can’t take it any more: “Lord, dost thou not care that my sister hath left me to serve alone? bid her therefore that she help me.” The answer is well known: “Martha, Martha, thou art careful and troubled about many things: But one thing is needful: and Mary hath chosen that good part, which shall not be taken away from her” (Luke 10:38–42).
Put this scene next to the tail.

ul: **The house and the meal are the Empress.** Martha welcomes the guest and busies herself with “much serving”. This is a real gift, and in the tail it stands at the root.
**“Hath left me to serve alone” is the name of the tail.** A lonely woman in a house full of people. You won’t find a more precise formula for 9-12-3.

**A request through a third party is the Hanged Man.** Notice: Martha doesn’t say to her sister, “Mary, help me.” She turns to the guest: “bid her”, and with a reproach too: “dost thou not care”. The familiar move is easy to recognise. A request that was never made to the person whose help is expected breaks out as a reproach, and to the wrong person.

**“One thing is needful” is the Hermit in his strong version.** Not many things, but one. In some of the oldest manuscripts the answer is even simpler: “few things are needed, or only one”. In other words, one dish would have been enough.

**“That good part” is the centre.** The word translated as “part” means a share in the Greek text, including a portion at a shared table. Mary got her portion at the guest’s feet. Martha, who cooked the whole feast, did not get hers. And “hath chosen” is a choice, which Wen sees as the main theme of the Lovers.

paragraphs: The parable does not divide people into right and wrong. In the Gospel of John the sisters’ story continues. When their brother Lazarus dies, “Martha, as soon as she heard that Jesus was coming, went and met him: but Mary sat still in the house” (John 11:20). Now it is Mary who stays sitting at home in her grief, and Martha who acts. These are not two types of people but two movements of one soul: to freeze and to go out to meet someone. The 9-12-3 tail has both. The trouble is that they switch on at the wrong time. At a party the person rushes about, and when they are hurting or need something themselves, they freeze.

**The 9-12-3 tail is a Martha who secretly wants to sit beside the guest, like Mary, but doesn’t allow herself to and doesn’t know how to ask.** The way out the parable suggests is not to stop cooking. It is to cook less, sit down sooner and tell your sister directly: “Help me.”
The scenes below are made-up examples, not a description of every person with this tail.
The tail is most often recognised by four storylines.

**Mothering a partner.** At first it is just care. She remembers when he has a doctor’s appointment, buys his clothes, sorts out his problems with relatives. Little by little the partner turns into a child, and you can’t be a couple with a child. A person with 9-12-3 ends up lonely in a couple precisely because they do everything for two. Manipura 6-6-12 says this in the language of numbers: love carried for two hangs in the air.

**“If he loves me, he’ll figure it out.”** The need is not named but shown: with a sigh, a tired look, a hint. The partner doesn’t understand what happened and gets resentment for something he didn’t know about. The Hanged Man works here in its pure form: waiting instead of asking.

**Love for someone who isn’t there.** A partner who is forever away: rotation shifts, business trips, another city. Or he is there, but not present, as in Pauline Boss’s second kind of ambiguous loss. Waiting becomes a form of love. For the Hermit such a partner is convenient: there is no need to open up, you can love at a distance, and the loneliness is justified by circumstances.

**A door closed after a hurt.** When the unspoken bills pile up, the Hermit switches on: “I don’t need anything from you.” The partner sees a chill that came out of nowhere and doesn’t know he has been handed a bill for years.

The strong version in all four storylines is the same — say what you need, directly and on time. And let yourself be cared for, even clumsily. Waite’s Lovers stand “unveiled before each other”. For this tail, opening up means showing not only love but also need.

For men with 9-12-3 the storyline is the same, only the household is different. He carries the family, works for two, fixes, drives, sorts things out and silently waits for it to be appreciated. He doesn’t talk about his own needs: “men don’t complain”. When there is no recognition, he retreats to the garage, into work, goes fishing — the Hermit with his lantern. And the accumulated bill sometimes bursts out in a flare-up that surprises everyone, himself included.

First, the main thing. The tail says nothing about pregnancy, infertility or whether you will have children. The sum of the numbers in a date knows nothing about the body. There is a motif of childlessness in the 9-12-3 legend, and the Empress at the root is, in Waite, “the door or gate by which an entrance is obtained into this life”. But the Empress’s fertility is wider than children. In Wen it is above all a card of creativity and fruition: of plans that come to life.

The tail is linked to Mum in a different way. The first Empress in a person’s life is whoever took care of them as a child. It is from them that a person learns whether the hostess sits down at her own table and whether it is all right to ask. Many people recognise in the description of 9-12-3 not themselves but their mum. And then, to their surprise, they notice that they are repeating her feast without its hostess.

A parent with 9-12-3 gives the children everything except one thing: an example of how to ask. Children whose mum never sits down at the table learn two things. Care is not asked for but waited for. And Mum is a function, not a person. When the children grow up, the tail often switches to the form of the Waiting One: she waits weeks for a call but doesn’t call herself, “so as not to impose”. Calling first and saying “I miss you” is the simplest way to break this script.

At work, 9-12-3 is recognised by invisible labour. Such a person remembers colleagues’ birthdays, finishes other people’s work, puts out fires management will never hear about, and for years doesn’t ask for a promotion. They wait to be noticed — that is the Hanged Man. For friends and acquaintances they work for free or almost for free, because naming a price is awkward. And when the invisible labour becomes too much, they leave suddenly and silently — that is the Hermit. To colleagues such a departure looks like a bolt from the blue.

The same trio has a strong side at work. Wen writes that the Empress suggests “an incredible gift for harnessing interpersonal relationships to yield success and harmony”: “She produces. She makes things happen.” The Hermit brings depth and the ability to work alone for a long time. The Hanged Man brings patience that knows how to wait for the harvest. The tail does well where results take a long time to ripen: in teaching and mentoring, medicine and care, the garden, the kitchen, crafts, research — anywhere people and projects don’t grow overnight. But if your work is caring for others, you need your own support too: someone you can complain to, days off that you don’t give away to anyone, and the right not to rescue everyone.

The storyline with money is similar. Money goes on others: the children, the parents, the shared table. For herself — “later”, “I don’t need it”, “the old one still works”. Manipura 6-6-12 adds one more feature. Big money decisions are made with an eye on the other person and stall while that person is silent. A useful question for 9-12-3: which of your purchases this month was made just for you, without benefiting anyone else?

paragraphs.h3: If someone close to you has 9-12-3

paragraphs: If you recognised your mum, wife, husband or colleague in this tail, here is what helps.

ul: **Don’t wait for a request.** It most likely won’t come. Make specific offers. Not “how can I help?” but “I’m doing the dishes, you sit down.”
**Don’t argue with “I’ll do it myself”.** Just do your part.
**Notice the invisible work out loud.** “You cooked for two days. Thank you.”
**Ask about their wishes.** “And what would you like?” — and wait for the answer, even if at first you hear “nothing”.
**Don’t believe a sudden “nothing”.** If someone has suddenly gone quiet and distant, there is most likely an unspoken request somewhere. Ask about it gently and without blame.

sections.h2: Solitude or withdrawal, care or sacrifice: how to tell them apart
paragraphs: Each card of the tail has a healthy version and a script version. From the outside they are easy to confuse. The questions below help to tell them apart.

**Solitude or withdrawal (the Hermit).** Wen distinguishes two cards in which a person turns inward. In the Four of Cups they turn inward “out of past disappointment” and “may be licking wounds”. In the Hermit, they do it to seek understanding.

ul: After time alone, do you come back to people with something — a thought, a decision, a request? Or do you go even deeper?
Do you withdraw to think, or so that nobody sees how tired and hurt you are?
When you are called back, do you feel relief, or annoyance that it took them so long to notice?

paragraphs: **A pause or a suspension (the Hanged Man).**

ul: Does your waiting have a deadline?
Are you waiting for something you could do or say yourself?
What will you do if nobody ever guesses?

paragraphs: **Care or sacrifice with a bill (the Empress and the Hanged Man).** Waite lists “selfishness” for the reversed Hanged Man, and Wen cautions not to confuse martyrdom with selfishness. Our reading: a sacrifice with a hidden bill is a deal the other side never signed.

ul: Can you give and never think about it again?
Does it hurt when you are not thanked?
Does the person you are caring for know that a response is expected of them?

paragraphs: **Faithfulness or freezing (the tail’s legend).**

ul: Does faithfulness to the past give you strength or take away the present?
Do you have “stopped clocks” — a decision you have been putting off ever since…?

Can you say of the person you are waiting for, in Pauline Boss’s terms, that they are “both there and gone”? Boss recommends exactly this kind of “both-and” thinking instead of “either-or”, so that grief and anger do not paralyse you.

sections.h2: What to do with the 9-12-3 tail: eight practices
paragraphs: These are the author’s exercises, drawn from the logic of the three cards — not a ritual and not a promise of results.

ol: **Ask before resentment sets in.** As soon as you notice you are waiting for someone to guess, you have 24 hours to say it directly. Say it to the person you are waiting on, not to a third party. Martha asked through the guest — and never got her help. A request made in time doesn’t have a chance to turn into a bill.

**Sit down first.** At any party you cook for, sit down at the table right at the start and eat the hot food while it is hot. Once a month, be a guest at your own table: someone else cooks and clears up, or the food is ordered in. The Empress on the card is sitting down.

**One dish.** Before a big effort, ask yourself: what is really needed here? One thing, not many. Do that one thing, and the rest only if you have the energy and the joy for it. “Few things are needed, or only one.”

**A deadline for waiting.** Every “I’ll wait” gets a date and an action after it. “If he doesn’t propose by the end of the month, I’ll tell him myself what I want.” “If my boss doesn’t raise the question by summer, I’ll go to him myself.” The Empress is a card of action and initiative. A deadline turns a suspension into a pause.

**An inventory of the silent bill.** Write down everyone you secretly consider your debtors, and for what. Next to each, put one of two words: “say” or “forgive”. An unspoken bill can’t be paid; it can only grow. You can either present it or close it.

**Solitude with a return.** You need solitude; it is a resource, not a breakdown. There is just one rule: come back from the quiet with something for people — a thought, a decision, a request. The Hermit’s light, according to Waite, means “where I am, you also may be.” The lantern is there so that people can come to you.

**Take without giving back.** When people help you, give you something or praise you, just say “thank you”. No “oh, you shouldn’t have”, no instant gift in return. The hanged man’s hands are tied behind his back. Freeing them means learning not only to give but also to take.

**Your own garden.** Start something that grows just for you: a plant, a craft, a course, a pleasure for the body. Everyone with this tail has the Empress as Muladhara’s Energy, and in Wen the cushions she sits on denote comfort. Abundance that never reaches the hostess makes a poor support.

paragraphs: And five phrases that break the script in the moment:

ul: Instead of “I’ll do it myself” — “help me with this”.
Instead of “I don’t need anything” — “I need…”.
Instead of “if he loves me, he’ll guess” — “it matters to me that…”.
Instead of “I do everything for you, and you…” — “what I’m missing is…”.
Instead of “in a minute, let me just bring out the main course” — “I’m sitting down”.

paragraphs: If loneliness keeps you from sleeping, working and enjoying life, if the waiting drags on for years and drains your strength, this is a task for a psychologist, not for the matrix. A reading of the tail gives you a language for observing yourself, but it does not replace professional help. For those who are waiting for someone missing or living next to a “psychologically absent” loved one, Pauline Boss’s book “Ambiguous Loss” may help.

sections.h2: The strength of 9-12-3: a hostess at her own table
paragraphs: In its worked-through version the tail gives a rare combination. Depth and the ability to be alone without fear — the Hermit. Patience that knows how to wait for what grows slowly — the Hanged Man. Abundance, warmth and a gift for creating places where others feel good — the Empress. And a capacity for real closeness — the Lovers in the centre. Such a person is good wherever results take a long time to ripen: in raising children and pupils, in the garden, in a craft, in any work that can’t be rushed.

You want to visit them. Their home is warm, the food is good and there is no need to pretend. They know the price of invisible care, because they paid it themselves for a long time, and so they are the first to notice whoever is washing the dishes while everyone else celebrates. They know how to spend time alone and come back from solitude with something for others. And at their own party they have a plate of their own.

Wen sees the archetype of the wounded healer in the Hanged Man and draws attention to a detail: the hanged man’s hands are hidden, which means “his ultimate offering to the world has yet to be seen”. For 9-12-3 this is perhaps the best hint. Hands tied behind the back can neither truly give nor take. Freeing them means learning both: holding out a plate and taking your own.

**A worked-through 9-12-3 is a hostess at her own table.** The feast has not become smaller, the care has not gone anywhere. It is just that among those who are cared for, the person has finally found a place too. That very “good part, which shall not be taken away”.

sections.h2: What this article is based on

ul: **Calculation** — the classic destiny matrix scheme with points A–T: D = A + B + C, E = A + B + C + D, M = D + E, N = D + M. The relationship line M–R1–R, where L = C + E, R = M + L, R1 = M + R. The money line L–R2–R, where R2 = L + R. The talent line B–P–K, where K = B + E, P = B + K. Rows of the energy chart: Manipura E–E, Svadhisthana L–M, Muladhara C–D; the third column is the reduced sum of the first two. Every sum greater than 22 is reduced by adding its digits. Frequencies by generation and year were obtained by going through all 46,298 dates from 1 January 1900 to 4 October 2026, and on every date the calculation was checked against the calculator’s engine. The “sum exactly 30” condition, the constant centre 6 and the absence of overlap with the “minus 22” rule were checked on all 73,414 dates from 1900 to 2100.

**Card meanings** — A. E. Waite, The Pictorial Key to the Tarot (1910, reissued 1922) and Benebell Wen, Holistic Tarot (2015). Quotes are given in the original English. Waite’s divinatory meanings are taken from the third part of his book and labelled as the divinatory list. The passage on prudence and the words the one thing needful come from the first part, from the section on the Hermit. Wen’s meanings for reversed cards apply to a Tarot spread, not to numbers calculated from a date. Wen gives Adelaide as a possible inspiration for the Empress only as speculation; the biographical dates follow publicly available sources.

**The parable** — the Gospel of Luke 10:38–42 and the Gospel of John 11:20, quoted from the King James Version. The reading “few things are needed, or only one” is found in Codex Vaticanus and Codex Sinaiticus. The parallel between the parable and the tail is ours.
**Ambiguous loss** — Pauline Boss, Ambiguous Loss: Learning to Live with Unresolved Grief (1999). The comparison with the tail’s legend is ours.
**Miss Havisham** — Charles Dickens, “Great Expectations” (1861).

**The name “the Lonely Woman” and the past-life legends** come from popular destiny matrix readings. Neither Waite nor Wen wrote about the matrix or karmic tails. Putting the three cards together into a script, the reading of the “two kinds of caution”, the arithmetic of the Empress, the forms of the Hostess, the Waiting One and the Recluse, and the practices are the author’s interpretation.
This is an esoteric model for self-reflection, not a forecast, a diagnosis or advice on health, money or relationships.

faq.q: Is the 9-12-3 tail a sentence to loneliness?
faq.a: No. The numbers are calculated from a birth date and do not predict events: neither divorce nor a lonely old age. The name “the Lonely Woman” is the title of a legend, not a forecast. Many people with 9-12-3 live in long marriages, raise children, are surrounded by friends — and still recognise themselves in the tail. It describes not marital status but a habit of coping alone and waiting in silence. And everyone with this tail has the Lovers, the card of the couple, in the centre of the chart. The tail speaks of what gets in the way of closeness, not of closeness never coming.

faq.q: What happened in a past life of someone with the 9-12-3 tail?
faq.a: Popular readings tell several legends. Most often it is about a woman whose beloved went missing: she did not know whether he had died or left her, and she rejected new love as a betrayal. There are versions about a nun, about a woman who sacrificed everything for a man and was left alone, about a domineering woman who suppressed her tenderness, about a closed person who kept their knowledge to themselves. These are legends of the tradition: neither numbers nor cards establish events of past lives. It is more useful to read them as a description of what is already visible now: love that waits instead of asking.

faq.q: Why “the Lonely Woman” if I’m a man?
faq.a: Gender plays no part in the calculation, and the meaning of the tail does not depend on it. The name comes from the legend and from the Empress at the root, but in Waite the Empress is “universal fecundity”, not the role of one gender. For men the script is the same: carrying everyone, silently waiting for recognition, retreating into work or the garage, and then flaring up from accumulated resentment. Popular readings advise women with 9-12-3 to “accept their femininity”, and men to “stop relying on women”. These are stereotypes, not arithmetic. The task of the tail is the same for everyone: to learn to ask and to take.

No. The tail says nothing about pregnancy or infertility, or about whether you will have children and how many. The motif of childlessness appears in one of the legends, and the Empress’s fertility in Wen is above all creative. If the subject of children is a painful one for you, that is a conversation for a doctor, not for the matrix. The tail’s theme is different: do you allow yourself the fruits of your own work — joy, rest, your own portion at the table?

faq.q: Is it true that with the 9-12-3 tail you need to “make peace with your mother”?
faq.a: This advice appears in almost every popular reading. It does have some support in the cards, but not the kind usually implied. Among the meanings of the reversed Empress, Wen mentions strained relations with a mother or a mother figure. But that is the meaning of a card drawn in a Tarot spread, and a number calculated from a date has no reversed position. So the tail does not oblige you to make peace or to forgive. The theme of the mother sounds in it for another reason: the first model of care a person sees is a mother’s. It is more useful not to “make peace” but to see whose care you are repeating, and decide what to keep from it. Sometimes that really does mean growing closer. Sometimes it means a boundary.

faq.q: I have 9-12-3 and a 6 in the centre — what does that mean?
faq.a: It is not a coincidence or a special case but a rule. 9-12-3 occurs only with the sum 30, and that always gives the centre 33 → 6. The Lovers in the centre are the comfort zone of this tail: closeness, mutuality, choice. The tail describes what keeps you from stepping into that closeness. There is more in the section on the hidden fourth card.

Yes, if these numbers stand on the bottom ray of your chart. 3-12-9 is the same tail read from the outer corner to the centre; some sites write it this way and call it “Female Loneliness”. The roles do not change: the Hermit is the entry, the Empress in the corner is the root. But if 3-12-9 stands on the top ray, that is the talent line. Everyone with 9-12-3 born in March has it there, and it should be read as talent.

All three have the Lovers in the centre and all three contain the Empress. In 9-3-21 (“the Overseer”) care works as the mechanism and turns into control, and the root is the World. In 18-3-12 (“Physical Suffering”) care is also the mechanism, used to drown out fear for the body, and the root is the Hanged Man. In 9-12-3 the Empress stands at the root and the Hanged Man in the middle. 18-3-12 teaches you to accept the pause, 9-12-3 to come out of it. By date, the sum of the three numbers tells them apart: 30 gives 9-12-3, 21 gives 9-3-21, and 12, 39 or 48 give 18-3-12.

faq.q: Why does another calculator show me a different tail?
faq.a: Usually because of the reduction rule. In the classic scheme, a sum greater than 22 is reduced by adding its digits: 30 → 3. Some calculators subtract 22 instead: 30 → 8. Under that rule the 9-12-3 tail also exists, but it goes to completely different dates. A search through all dates from 1900 to 2100 found not a single one that gets 9-12-3 under both rules. The classic result is easy to check by hand: the day arcanum, the month and the year arcanum must add up to exactly 30.

faq.q: Is 9-12-3 in the relationship line or the money line also a tail?
faq.a: No. A karmic tail is only the trio on the bottom ray, in the order M–N–D. The same numbers in the relationship line M–R1–R or in the money line L–R2–R are a programme of that channel, and they are read by its roles. In the relationship line, 9-12-3 occurs for holders of this tail born in years with arcanum 15 (1905, 1914, 1923, 1932, 1941 and 1950). It also occurs for some holders of the 9-15-6, 9-3-21, 9-9-18 and 9-18-9 tails — all the tails whose entry is also the Hermit. In the money line, 9-12-3 is found only with tails that begin with 21: 21-4-10, 21-10-16, 21-7-13 and 21-10-7. Never with 9-12-3 itself.

The numbers are calculated from your birth date and don’t change. What changes is how the script plays out. Signs of a worked-through tail: you speak about your needs in time and to the person you are expecting help from. You accept help and are in no hurry to pay it back at once. Your waiting has deadlines. You come back from solitude with words, not with resentment. The silent bill, if there was one, has been said out loud or crossed out. And at your own party, you sit at the table. Then the tail remains a description of your strengths, not a story that keeps repeating.

faq.q: What should I do if my child has 9-12-3?
faq.a: There are fewer such children than adults: among those born from 2000 to 2025, one child in 29 has 9-12-3. In 2026 the year arcanum equals 10, and the tail goes to children whose day arcanum and month add up to 20. That makes 16 dates: 19 January, 18 February, 17 March, 16 April, 15 May, 14 June, 13 July, 12 August, 11 and 29 September, 10 and 28 October, 9 and 27 November, 8 and 26 December. A child with 9-12-3 especially needs three things. The first is the experience that asking is allowed and that requests get answered. Praise them not only for helping but also for asking: “It’s great that you told me what you need.” The second is the right to be a child, not a little helper. If they are praised mostly for helping, looking after the younger ones and never asking for anything, they will quickly learn that love is earned by service. The third is the right to withdraw into themselves, but with a way back. The Hermit needs quiet, and there is no need to take it away by force. But after the quiet, ask: “What was going on with you? What do you need?” That is how a child learns that people come back from solitude with words, not with resentment. And most important of all is example. Children see whether Mum sits down at her own table.

report: The 9-12-3 tail is called “the Lonely Woman”, yet its loneliness usually plays out in a house full of people. Men and women get it equally, and many who have it are long married, raising children, surrounded by friends — and still recognise themselves. It is loneliness among one’s own: the person feeds everyone, waits, endures, and says nothing about their own needs.

Still, the name is exact, and it reads straight off the cards. “Lonely” is the Hermit at the entry, a figure standing alone. “Woman” is the Empress at the root, Waite’s “fruitful mother of thousands”. Between them hangs the Hanged Man, keeping them apart. The tail tells how home, care and love get cut off from the one who creates them.

The most detailed past-life legend tells of a woman whose beloved went missing: she never learned whether he had died or left her. The legend cannot be checked, but its plot has a name in psychology. In the 1970s Pauline Boss talked with the wives of pilots missing in action in Vietnam and called their state ambiguous loss: no grieving — he might be alive; no moving on — he might come back. Even more familiar is its second kind: someone close is physically present but psychologically absent. Our reading: the legend is less about a past life than about loneliness in this one.

In Waite’s divinatory lists the Hermit has “prudence, circumspection” and the Hanged Man “wisdom, circumspection, discernment”. The two cards share a word: circumspection. The Empress, by contrast, opens with “fruitfulness, action, initiative”: not to look around, but to begin.

Our reading. The circumspection of people with 9-12-3 is real. But before giving birth to anything — a request, a wish, a celebration of their own — they check twice. “What if they say no?” is the Hermit. “I’ll wait, maybe they’ll guess” is the Hanged Man. While the checking goes on, the moment passes. **The tail’s entry and mechanism are two cautions in a row. Its root is a card that is never cautious.**

report.h3: A feast where the hostess never sits down

report: The scene is invented and does not describe everyone. It is Mum’s milestone birthday, twelve guests, and as always Lena is cooking. Her sister offered to bring salads, her husband asked what to buy: “No need, I’ll do it myself, it’s quicker.” This is the Hermit: take everything personal inside and cope alone.

At the party Lena doesn’t sit down: “In a minute, just let me bring out the main course.” She is waiting for the others to see how much she has done and head for the sink themselves. This is the Hanged Man. Her hands are like the hanged man’s on Waite’s card, tied behind the back — hands that can neither take a plate nor ask. The party goes on in the living room, she is in the kitchen, and a tally is growing inside: “nobody offered”. The sacrifice is silent, but not free.

And the party is a success: everyone is fed, Mum is happy, the guests praise the pie. This is the Empress, the tail’s real gift: around such a person everything grows. But the abundance reaches everyone except the hostess. In Wen, “the pillows that the Empress rests on denote comfort”. The Empress rests. The hostess of this tail does not.

That evening Lena washes up alone. “What’s wrong?” — “Nothing.” The bill is never presented, so nobody can pay it. The tail concludes: asking is pointless, easier to do it herself — and the circle starts again. **Loneliness here is made not of absent people but of unspoken requests.**

report.h3: A tail made entirely of the Empress

report: Everyone with 9-12-3 has the Lovers in the centre of the matrix, the comfort zone: the most coupled card in the deck, in Waite two figures “unveiled before each other”. So this tail’s loneliness is not character but script: the person blossoms in mutuality; the script keeps them out of it.

And the whole tail is built from the Empress. The Lovers in the centre are 33, Empress plus Empress: 3 + 3 = 6. The Hermit is Empress plus Lovers, 3 + 6 = 9. The Hanged Man is Empress plus Hermit, 3 + 9 = 12. Our reading: two kinds of care that meet make love; care that finds no answer turns inward and hangs in the air. People withdraw into this loneliness not from a lack of love but from a surplus with nowhere to go. **The 9-12-3 tail doesn’t need to learn to love. It needs to learn to take.**

Waite himself provides the key to the parable: true prudence, he writes of the Hermit, “is concerned with the one thing needful”. The words come from Luke’s story of Martha and Mary; the parallel with the tail is ours. Martha “was cumbered about much serving”, while Mary “sat at Jesus’ feet, and heard his word”. Martha finally snaps: “Lord, dost thou not care that my sister hath left me to serve alone? bid her therefore that she help me.”

A lonely woman in a house full of people. And a request routed through a third party: not to her sister but to the guest, with a reproach attached. The answer: “Martha, Martha, thou art careful and troubled about many things: But one thing is needful: and Mary hath chosen that good part, which shall not be taken away from her.” In the Greek, “part” means a share, including a portion at a shared table. Mary got hers. Martha, who cooked the whole feast, did not.

**The 9-12-3 tail is a Martha who secretly wants to sit beside the guest, like Mary, but doesn’t allow herself to and doesn’t know how to ask.** The way out is not to stop cooking but to cook less, sit down sooner and tell her sister plainly: “Help me.” In practice:

ul: once “let them guess” creeps in, say it plainly within a day, to the person concerned, not a third party;
at one’s own party, sit down first and eat the hot food while it is hot;
give every “I’ll wait” a deadline: it turns suspension into a pause;
meet help, a gift or praise with a plain “thanks”, not “oh, there was no need”.

report: If loneliness gets in the way of sleep, work and joy, if the waiting drags on for years and drains strength, this is a task for a psychologist, not for the matrix.

report.h3: Hands that know how to take

report: In the worked-through version, this is someone people love to visit: a warm home, good food, no need to pretend. Such a person can be alone without fear and wait for what grows slowly. They know the price of invisible care and are the first to notice whoever is washing up while everyone else celebrates.

Wen notes that the hanged man’s hands are hidden: “his ultimate offering to the world has yet to be seen”. Hands tied behind the back can neither truly give nor take. Freeing them means learning both: holding out a plate and taking one’s own.

**A worked-through 9-12-3 is a hostess at her own table.** The feast is no smaller, the care has not gone anywhere. It is just that among those being cared for, the person has finally found a place too — that very “good part, which shall not be taken away”.
